paragraphs.text: [Ya Shi Xiang](dancong:ya-shi-xiang), duck dung, is the market name for one Dancong line, traced to Pingkengtou village. Most lists of the ten [classic types](dancong:aromas) leave it out, though it sells widely. In 2014 the name Yinhua Xiang, silver flower, was put forward for it, but many sellers keep the old one. Three stories explain that name, and all are told only as stories: that it was chosen to keep thieves away from the bush, that it comes from the yellow local soil called duck dung soil, and that duck droppings lay on the bush.

The leaf is [Phoenix Dancong](dancong:definition), the oolong of Phoenix Mountain in Chao'an, Chaozhou, in eastern Guangdong. [Dancong](dancong:name) means single bush, though a named line today is mostly grown from cuttings or grafts of one chosen bush. The leaf is withered in the sun, then [shaken and rested in rounds](dancong:making) to bruise its edges, fixed fast at high heat, rolled into long strips, dried and roasted. This is a 2026 tea. Freshly roasted Dancong is [rested for some months](dancong:ageing) before it is ready, and the trade does not agree on how many.

brewing.text: Brew it gongfu style in a small gaiwan or clay pot, with about 3 to 8 grams for 100 to 120 ml and hot water, about 88 to 100°C; Chinese accounts mostly say 95 to 100°C. A quick rinse is common. Steeps start at a few seconds and grow a few seconds each round, and a good Dancong gives about eight to fifteen. Too long, too hot or too much leaf and it turns bitter and astringent.

notice.text: Flowers above all, a sweetness that comes back after swallowing, a high scent that lasts, honey, often ripe fruit such as peach, and what the trade calls mountain rhyme, shan yun; a liquor from golden to orange-red or amber.
